subject: diplomatic-appointments-lqa
note: 5A, 2026-10-02, against the first reading print (Senate) of 7 September 2026. Every place found while encoding where the text supports two readings that change an outcome. Reading A is taken in every case and is what the L4's plain rules and the console scheme follow; reading B is a rule whose name says 'reading B'. cases.l4 asserts both readings on the facts that divide them. A fork is not a finding: whether the drafter left the choice open is for 7A (category U).

entries.question: Where does 'the last 10 years' begin, so that a membership that ended exactly 10 years before the day in question is, or is not, 'within the last 10 years'?

readings.reading: The 10 years end at the end of the day in question and, by analogy with Acts Interpretation Act s 2G(2) (120 months), begin at the start of the same date 10 years before the next day; a last day as a member on the anniversary date is outside them. The person has a significant, not a disqualifying, affiliation.
The 10 years take in the anniversary date itself, so a last day of membership exactly 10 years earlier is within them, and the person is disqualified for one more day.

entries.why: The Acts Interpretation Act defines a month (s 2G) and the way a period of months runs, but not a year; reading 10 years as 120 months and running the period back from the end of the day in question is the nearest statutory guide. Neither the Bill nor the EM addresses the boundary.
entries.asserted: cases.l4: Blair (last day 15 June 2018, tested 15 June 2028) is not disqualified on A and is on B; Blair's twin (last day 16 June 2018) is disqualified on A. Section 8(2)(a) is asserted on both readings.

entries.question: Does 'employed under the Members of Parliament (Staff) Act 1984 as a member of the staff of a person occupying' a listed position include an electorate employee of that person, or only staff employed by virtue of the position?

readings.reading: Any employment under the MOP(S) Act by an employing individual who occupied a listed position while the person was so employed, including an electorate employee (MOP(S) Act s 11(1)) of a Minister or shadow Minister.
Only personal employees (Ministerial, s 11(2), or non-Ministerial, s 11(3)) employed in the employer's capacity as holder of the position; electorate employees do not count.

entries.why: The words describe the employer ('a person occupying'), not the capacity in which the person was employed; MOP(S) Act s 3AA makes the parliamentarian the employing individual for electorate employees too. EM para 12 ('has worked (or works) for a ... minister or shadow minister') is consistent with A. Reading B matters most for a shadow Minister, who without a MOP(S) Act s 4 determination can employ only electorate employees.
entries.asserted: cases.l4: Finley (electorate employee of a Minister) and Indy (electorate employee of a shadow Minister) have the affiliation on A and not on B; Gray (personal employee of the Prime Minister) has it on both.

entries.question: When must the party be 'a registered political party (within the meaning of the Commonwealth Electoral Act 1918)': while the person was its officer or employee, or on the day the question is asked?

readings.reading: The party must have been registered under Part XI of the Commonwealth Electoral Act while the person held the role.
The party must be registered on the day the question is asked, whether or not it was when the person held the role.

entries.why: 'is or has been an officer or employee of a registered political party' describes the person's past role, and the party's character at that time is what gave the role its political significance. Reading B would attach the affiliation to a past role in an unregistered body once the body later registers, and drop it when a party deregisters.
entries.asserted: cases.l4: Jordan (officer of a party unregistered then, registered now) has no significant affiliation on A and has one on B.

entries.question: Which Selection Committees count towards 'no recommendation ... has been made by a Selection Committee established for the purpose' and 'at least two such Selection Committees have instead referred the matter back' (s 9(3)), and towards 'that particular appointment' (s 10(6)): those for the current vacancy only, or every Committee ever established for an appointment to the office?

readings.reading: Only Committees established for the current vacancy, after the previous appointment to the office was made.
Every Committee ever established for an appointment to the office, including Committees for earlier vacancies.

entries.why: s 10(7) and its note ('historical recommendations cannot be relied on for subsequent appointments') treat each appointment as its own process; s 10(6) speaks of 'that particular appointment'. On reading B one recommendation ever made for an office would close s 9(3) for the office for good, and referrals for a filled vacancy would open it for the next.
entries.asserted: cases.l4: Italy (two referrals for the vacancy filled in 2027, none since) does not meet s 9(3)(a), (b) on A and does on B; the 2028 Committee's list of five is permitted on A and not on B (s 10(6)).

entries.question: In 'within 7 days of establishing a Selection Committee', is the day of establishment one of the 7 days?

readings.reading: No: the 7 days begin on the day after the Committee is established, so the last day is the 7th day after it (then Acts Interpretation Act s 36(2)).
Yes: the 7 days include the day of establishment, so the last day is the 6th day after it (then s 36(2)).

entries.why: Acts Interpretation Act s 36(1) has no item for 'within N days of' an event; items 5 and 6 (a period beginning from or after a day excludes that day) and the common-law rule excluding the day of the event both point to A.
entries.asserted: cases.l4: a Committee established Tuesday 11 January 2028 and given its list Tuesday 18 January is in time on A and late on B; a second case shows s 36(2) carrying a Sunday last day to Monday.

entries.question: Must the candidate a Selection Committee 'agrees on' and recommends be one of those on the Minister's list?

readings.reading: Yes: 'a candidate for the appointment' in s 10(3)(a) is one of the 'proposed candidates' on the s 10(1) list.
No: the Committee may agree on any person, including one it found through the assistance or information s 10(4) lets it seek.

entries.why: The list's limits in s 10(2) (no disqualified candidate; a cap on affiliated candidates; reasons for each) would be pointless if the Committee could recommend someone off it. EM para 23 ('identify a candidate from that list') reads it as A. Nothing in s 10(3) says so expressly.
entries.asserted: cases.l4: a Committee votes 3-0 for Zed, who is not on the list: it agrees on Zed on B, not on A, and makes no recommendation on A.

entries.question: Is 'a majority of the votes of the members' a majority of all 3 members' votes, or of the votes cast?

readings.reading: A majority of the members' votes: at least 2 of the 3 members must vote for the question.
A majority of the votes cast: abstentions do not count, so 1 vote for and none against carries.

entries.why: 'of the members' (not 'of the members present and voting', the usual phrase for votes cast) and the quorum of all 3 members in s 13(2) point to A. EM paras 23 and 33 ('at least two committee members must concur'; 'two or more votes in favour') read it so.
entries.asserted: cases.l4: a meeting with 1 vote for, none against and 2 abstentions does not carry the question on A and does on B; the Committee agrees on the candidate on B only.

entries.question: Does a Selection Committee 'agree on a candidate' when the question is carried by a majority under s 13(3), or only when all three members agree?

readings.reading: When the question of recommending the candidate is carried by a majority under s 13(3) at a quorate meeting.
Only when all 3 members agree: 'agrees' in s 10(3)(a) means unanimity, and anything less is 'otherwise' and a referral.

entries.why: s 13(1) makes the decision under s 10(3) a decision at a meeting, and s 13(3) says how a question at a meeting is determined; reading B would leave s 13(3) nothing to do for the Committee's one decision. EM para 23 reads it as A. The ordinary meaning of 'agrees' supports B.
entries.asserted: cases.l4: the Japan Committee's 2-1 vote for Alex is agreement on A and not on B.

entries.question: Must the person a Selection Committee recommends be appointed?

readings.reading: No: s 9(2) only makes the recommended person one who may be appointed (s 9(1) 'may be appointed ... only if'). Nothing in the operative provisions obliges anyone to make the appointment.
Yes: the simplified outline (s 3: 'any person so recommended by the Selection Committee must be appointed') and EM para 18 ('The Minister must accept this recommendation') state a duty.

entries.why: s 3 is a simplified outline and not operative (OPC Drafting Direction 1.3A; approved scope); the operative words of s 9 are permissive. Reading B rests on the outline and the EM alone. The gap between them is a category X question for 7A.
entries.asserted: cases.l4: on the Japan facts (a recommendation of Alex in effect) the duty rule is FALSE on A and TRUE on B.

entries.question: Is s 9(3)(c)(i) met when the Minister is satisfied the person has no significant political affiliation but the person in fact has one?

readings.reading: Yes: the condition is the Minister's state of satisfaction, a fact; whether the person in truth has an affiliation does not enter it (subject to the usual limits on a satisfaction being reasonably formed).
No: the Minister must be satisfied and the person must in fact have no significant political affiliation on the day of appointment.

entries.why: The text makes satisfaction the condition, where s 9(1)(a) and s 11(2) state objective conditions; a satisfaction formula is ordinarily read as a jurisdictional fact of opinion. On A an appointment of an affiliated person on a mistaken satisfaction complies with s 9 and s 14(3) does not bite.
entries.asserted: cases.l4: Finley (an affiliation under s 8(2)(b) on FORK-02 A) appointed on the Minister's satisfaction meets s 9(3)(c)(i) on A and not on B.

entries.question: Must both Houses have passed their resolutions approving the appointment before it is made?

readings.reading: Yes: s 9(1) asks whether s 9(3) applies when the person 'may be appointed', so both resolutions must have been passed by the day of the appointment.
No: 'both Houses of Parliament pass a resolution approving the person's appointment' can be met after the event, approving an appointment already made.

entries.why: s 9(1) is a condition on the power to appoint, tested when the power is used; EM para 19 ('the Minister cannot make the appointment until both Houses of Parliament have passed a resolution') reads it so. 'approving the person's appointment' is apt for either.
entries.asserted: cases.l4: Blair's appointment with the House resolving four days after it does not meet s 9(3)(c)(ii) on A and does on B.

entries.question: When the Minister is satisfied under s 9(3)(c)(i) and both Houses have also approved the appointment under s 9(3)(c)(ii), is the person appointed 'because the Minister is satisfied', so that a statement of reasons must be tabled?

readings.reading: Yes: the appointment rests on s 9(3) and s 9(3)(c)(i) is met, so the statement is required whether or not (c)(ii) is also met.
No: where both Houses have approved, the appointment is made because of their resolutions and no statement is required.

entries.why: 'because' identifies the ground relied on, and the Minister's satisfaction remains a ground although another also exists; reading A keeps the transparency the tabling requirement serves. The text does not address two grounds at once.
entries.asserted: cases.l4: Alex, appointed after two referrals with the Minister satisfied and both Houses approving, needs a statement on A and not on B.

entries.question: In 'within 5 sitting days of that House after the appointment is made', does a sitting of the House on the day of the appointment (after it is made) count as one of the 5?

readings.reading: No: the sitting days counted are those after the day the appointment is made.
Yes: a sitting on the day of the appointment, after the appointment is made, is the first of the 5.

entries.why: Acts Interpretation Act s 36(1) items 5 and 6 (a period beginning after a day excludes it), by analogy, and the day-granularity of 'sitting day' (s 2M) favour counting whole sitting days after the day of the appointment. The words 'after the appointment is made' tie the start to an event, not a day, which supports B.
entries.asserted: cases.l4: the Senate sat on 1 September 2028, the day of the India appointment; the statement tabled on 11 September (the 5th later sitting) is in time on A and late (the 6th) on B.

entries.question: If a person who had no affiliation when the acting arrangement was made comes to have one while acting, must the arrangement be terminated?

readings.reading: No: s 14(4) is broken only by an arrangement 'made' otherwise than in accordance with the Act, which is tested when it is made; s 11(2) is not breached in a way s 14(6) reaches by a later affiliation.

Yes: s 11(2) ('must not have') is a continuing requirement, and once the chargé d'affaires has an affiliation the arrangement must be terminated under s 14(6) as soon as practicable after the Minister becomes aware.

entries.why: s 14(4) and (6) speak of the making of the arrangement; s 11(2) is in the present tense and EM para 15 speaks of a person 'acting' who 'has' an affiliation, which supports B. A leaves a later affiliation with no consequence; B gives s 11(2) a duty with no stated trigger.
entries.asserted: cases.l4: Morgan, acting from 1 February 2028, becomes a party officer on 1 May 2028; on 1 June the arrangement need not be terminated on A and must be on B (and need not be on 30 April on either).

entries.question: Does s 15 ('This Act applies in relation [to] an appointment made on or after the commencement ... if the term of the appointment starts at least 12 months after that commencement') also limit the Act's application to acting arrangements?

readings.reading: No: s 15 speaks only of appointments; an acting arrangement is not an appointment (s 11(3) keeps it out of s 9), so the Act governs every arrangement made from commencement.
Yes: an acting arrangement is an 'appointment' for s 15, so arrangements made in the first 12 months after commencement are outside the Act.

entries.why: The Bill uses 'appointment' and 'arrangement for a person to act' as distinct terms throughout s 14; s 15 uses only the first. EM para 35 says the 12 months allow 'preparations necessary for the implementation of the framework', which does not need to delay s 11, as no Committee is involved.
entries.asserted: cases.l4: Finley acting from 1 June 2027 (3 months after commencement) breaches the Act on A and is outside it on B.

entries.question: Is an appointment made 'otherwise than in accordance with this Act' when s 9(1) is met but the process behind the recommendation broke ss 10 or 12 (a late list, a list over its affiliated-candidate cap, a late notice, a Committee established while another existed)?

readings.reading: No: an appointment is in accordance with the Act when s 9(1) permits it (and s 15 and s 7 are as they are). Breaches of ss 10 and 12 are breaches by the Minister or the Committee of their own duties, with no consequence for the appointment.

Yes: 'in accordance with this Act' takes in the whole process for the appointment, so any breach of ss 10 or 12 for a Committee for this vacancy makes the appointment one that s 14(3) requires to be terminated.

entries.why: s 9 is the provision that governs the making of an appointment, and s 14(1) is aimed at the appointment, not the process. On either reading a decision not made at a quorate meeting is no recommendation at all (s 13), so it fails s 9(2). Reading B gives ss 10 and 12, which otherwise have no stated consequence, the s 14(3) sanction.
entries.asserted: cases.l4: the Canada appointment (list given 14 days after establishment, with 2 affiliated candidates of 4; recommendation 3-0) is in accordance with the Act on A and must be terminated on B; the Japan appointment complies on both.
